title: Thyroid nodule: applied neck anatomy

header.contentArea: Surgical anatomy: thyroid gland relationships and nodule assessment

thyroid nodule: ultrasound and cytology reports

brief.scenario: An adult has a lower anterior neck swelling that moves on swallowing and persistent hoarseness.
brief.task: Describe the thyroid's anatomical relationships and explain the implications for assessment and surgery. You have 9 minutes. The examiner will ask questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Locate it, relate it, then give the surgical consequence of each relationship.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Saying hoarseness means the cancer has invaded the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Check for airway compromise, then describe the gland and its fascial attachment.

flow: Assessing the nodule and the hoarse voice
Nerve and parathyroid risks at surgery

grid.label: Describes the gland and why it moves on swallowing
grid.fail: Describes the thyroid in isolation and cannot explain movement on swallowing.
grid.pass: Isthmus over the upper tracheal rings, lobes beside larynx and trachea, enclosed by pretracheal fascia, so it moves on swallowing.
grid.high: Links these features to examination: movement on swallowing, retrosternal extension and tracheal deviation.

grid.label: Gives the surrounding relations
grid.fail: Omits the posterior and lateral relations.
grid.pass: Strap muscles in front, carotid sheath laterally, trachea and oesophagus medially, parathyroids and recurrent laryngeal nerves posteriorly.
grid.high: Turns each relation into a symptom or risk: stridor, dysphagia, voice change.

grid.label: Recognises concerning features
grid.fail: Diagnoses cancer from one physical finding, or dismisses the hoarseness.
grid.pass: Recognises a hard or fixed lump, cervical lymphadenopathy, voice change or compressive symptoms as concerning.
grid.high: States that hoarseness raises concern but does not establish recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion.

grid.label: Plans assessment of the hoarse voice
grid.fail: Attributes the hoarseness to nerve invasion and plans routine follow-up, or reassures.
grid.pass: Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for thyroid cancer (NICE NG12, rec 1.8.5), with neck ultrasound and assessment of vocal-fold mobility.
grid.high: Assesses any airway compromise immediately before arranging further assessment.

grid.label: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
grid.fail: Cannot name the nerve to cricothyroid or where it is at risk.
grid.pass: At risk at the superior thyroid pedicle; injury impairs cricothyroid function and pitch control.
grid.high: Explains the voice change may be subtle, affecting pitch and projection, so it is easily missed.

grid.label: Parathyroid glands
grid.fail: Forgets the parathyroids or the risk to calcium.
grid.pass: Preserves the parathyroid glands and their vascular supply to reduce postoperative hypocalcaemia.
grid.high: Notes the inferior thyroid artery supplies most parathyroids and plans postoperative calcium checks.

grid.label: Links anatomy to operative risk
grid.fail: Lists structures without saying why they matter.
grid.pass: For each structure states where it is, what it does and what happens if it is injured.
grid.high: Summarises the operative risks a patient needs to hear for consent: voice change, hypocalcaemia, bleeding.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It is a butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that makes thyroxine.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The trachea is behind it. I am not sure about the rest.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He has a nodule and persistent hoarseness. What does that mean?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It means the cancer has invaded the recurrent laryngeal nerve, so this is definitely malignant.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would review him in clinic in a few months.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What else is at risk at thyroid surgery?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Bleeding. I cannot think of anything else.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The isthmus lies over the upper tracheal rings and the lobes lie beside the larynx and trachea. It is enclosed by pretracheal fascia, so it moves on swallowing.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: In front are the strap muscles, laterally the carotid sheath, medially the trachea and oesophagus, and posteriorly the parathyroids and recurrent laryngeal nerves.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: He has a nodule and persistent hoarseness. What does that mean?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A hard or fixed lump, nodes, voice change or compressive symptoms are concerning, but no single finding makes the diagnosis.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Persistent hoarseness with a thyroid nodule raises concern for vocal-fold dysfunction and possible malignancy, but does not establish recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion. Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for thyroid cancer (NICE NG12, rec 1.8.5), with neck ultrasound and appropriate assessment of vocal-fold mobility; assess any airway compromise immediately.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It is at risk at the superior thyroid pedicle, and injury impairs cricothyroid function and pitch control.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would preserve the parathyroid glands and their vascular supply to reduce postoperative hypocalcaemia.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: For each structure: where it is, what it does, and what happens if I injure it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It is enclosed by pretracheal fascia, so the swelling moves on swallowing. I would also look for retrosternal extension and tracheal deviation on examination.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Each relation explains a symptom: tracheal compression gives stridor, oesophageal compression dysphagia, and the posterior nerves voice change.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He has a nodule and persistent hoarseness. What does that mean?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: First I would ask about breathing and listen for stridor; assess any airway compromise immediately.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Persistent hoarseness with a thyroid nodule raises concern for vocal-fold dysfunction and possible malignancy, but does not establish recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion. Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for thyroid cancer (NICE NG12, rec 1.8.5), with neck ultrasound and appropriate assessment of vocal-fold mobility.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is at risk at the superior thyroid pedicle; injury impairs cricothyroid function and pitch control. The change can be subtle, affecting pitch and projection rather than causing obvious hoarseness.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Preserve the parathyroid glands and their vascular supply to reduce postoperative hypocalcaemia. Most are supplied by the inferior thyroid artery, so I would plan postoperative calcium checks.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: When consenting, I would explain the main risks these relationships create: voice change, low calcium and bleeding.

failures.move: Tells the patient hoarseness proves nerve invasion by cancer.
failures.consequence: Overstates the diagnosis before any assessment.

failures.move: Arranges routine follow-up for persistent hoarseness with a nodule.
failures.consequence: Delays assessment of possible malignancy and the airway.

failures.move: Forgets the parathyroid glands and their blood supply.
failures.consequence: Misses the cause of postoperative hypocalcaemia.

knowledge.fact: Pretracheal fascia encloses the gland, which is why a thyroid swelling moves on swallowing.
Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for thyroid cancer in people with an unexplained thyroid lump.
Greyscale ultrasound with an established grading system is the initial diagnostic test for thyroid nodules.
Persistent hoarseness with a nodule raises concern for vocal-fold dysfunction and possible malignancy; it does not establish nerve invasion.
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is at risk at the superior thyroid pedicle; injury impairs cricothyroid function and pitch control.
Preserve the parathyroid glands and their vascular supply to reduce postoperative hypocalcaemia.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve course and injury are covered in MB-487.

recall.think: Airway first if the voice or breathing has changed.
recall.say: “Hoarseness raises concern but does not prove nerve invasion.”
do: Consider suspected cancer pathway referral (NG12 1.8.5); neck ultrasound

numbers.meaning: recurrent laryngeal (voice) and external branch of the superior laryngeal (pitch)

recall.trap: Describing the gland without the consequence of each relation.
recall.finish: Protect the nerves and the parathyroids and their blood supply.

push.question: Why does the swelling move on swallowing?
What lies posterior and lateral to each lobe?
What makes a thyroid swelling concerning?
He has persistent hoarseness. What do you do?
push.expect: Airway first; consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (NG12 1.8.5), ultrasound, vocal-fold mobility.

push.question: What nerve supplies cricothyroid, and where is it at risk?
What structure must be preserved to maintain calcium regulation?

curveballs.prompt: So the hoarseness means the nerve is invaded?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not necessarily: it raises concern for vocal-fold dysfunction and possible malignancy; assess vocal-fold mobility.
